full_judgment:
4. The prosecution in order to prove the charge examined 13 witnesses in the absence of the convict appellant and on 13-10-2008 he had surrendered in the trial Court with a petition for cross-examining those PWs 1-13 who were examined in his absence and the said petition was allowed and most of the witnesses were later on cross-examined by the convict appellant. The prosecution also examined 2(two) witnesses in presence of the appellant, thus the prosecution examined 15 witnesses in all and on completion of the recording of evidence the convict appellant was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure when he pleaded his innocence and disclosed his unwillingness to adduce any defence witness. 

 7. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record found the appellant guilty and convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid and the convict appellant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment preferred this appeal in this Court and the appeal is opposed by the respondent No.2. 

 8. Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, the learned senior Advocate with Mr Md Shamsul Alam appearing on behalf of the convict appellant supporting the appeal and opposing the judgment of the trial Court submits that the trial Court erred both in law and facts in finding the appellant guilty. The trial Court should have considered that there is no material in the hands of the prosecution to show that the accused had misappropriated the goods in question. There is no evidence in the record that he had taken the goods for his personal gain or he allowed anybody to take away the said goods from the shed and in fact the security system of the port shed did not allow anybody to take any goods from the shed which is a very secured place and co. trolled by the various types, of the customs officers. 

 10. The learned Advocate also submits that after lodging the FIR when the remaining goods were returned back to the importer through his agent the importer was convinced that there should not be any case against the accused appellant and with a view to get rid of the accused the informant had sworn an affidavit stating that he has no any allegation against the accused and he is not interested to proceed with the case but the investigating agencies without taking into notice of the said fact and affidavit submitted charge sheet for the reason best known to them. 

 17. In respect of affidavit sworn by the. informant the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2 submits that since the offence was not a compoundable offence, the informant had no any authority to settle the matter with the accused and the informant very illegally had sworn the affidavit to give some advantage to the accused for the reasons best known to the informant but that was not binding upon the Investigating Officer or upon the Court. She also submits that when any offence is compoundable everyone should appreciate the settlement of dispute outside of the court but whenever the offence is not compoundable no one should be insisted or encouraged to resolve the problem without the intervention of the Court. So, defying the affidavit sworn by the inform-ant neither the investigating agency nor the Court committed no illegality. 

 18. Now, in respect of the merit of the case, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2 submits that the written endorsement of the convict appellant that he would return back 2,310 kgs iron scrap to the informant party is the best evidence to prove his guilt. So, the other evidence in this case was immaterial but even then the prosecution examining as many as 15 witnesses in this case has been able to prove the charge as framed against the appellant and the trial Court being convinced of the evidences of those witnesses rightly found that the accused had received 19,000 kgs iron scrap in his custody but at the time of delivery he could have returned back only 17,590 kgs iron scrap. So, the accused appellant had misappropriated the remaining 2,310 kgs iron scrap and the trial Court rightly found that the accused had misappropriated the said scrap. 

 19. The learned Advocate also submits that there is no any evidence in the record to show that the system of the godown or shed did not allow anybody to bring out any goods from the shed. So, there is no scope at this stage to say that the appellant was not in a position to bring out the said scrap outside of the shed. 

 20. She also submits that in this case most of the witnesses were examined from the Benapole Port authority Who has been serving there but there is nothing in their such evidence that it is difficult for anybody to takeout any goods from the shed. So, the arguments of the learned Advocate for the appellant has no legs to stand that it is impossible for anybody to bring out any goods from the shed. 

 22. She lastly submits that the appellant has been trying to bank the evidence of Benod Biswas, the C&F agent who stated that some goods have been delivered later on but this evidence of Benod Biswas has not been corroborated by his principle PW 1 Sadhan Kumar Sarker, the informant of this case. So, there is no any prove in the record to show that some of the goods were delivered later on to the importer; So, the trial Court did not commit any error of law and fact in finding the appellant guilty under section 409 of the Penal Code and 5(2) of the Prevention Of Corruption Act. So, the judgment of the trial Court did not call for any interference from this Court. 

 23. I have considered the above submissions and the arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record particularly the FIR, the evidence, the judgment of the trial Court and other materials on record. 

 24. From the arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties it appears to me that the main arguments of the learned Advocate for the appellant is that if the prosecution case is taken as a fact in its entirety that did not disclose any case of misappropriation as the accused had no any intention to misappropriate the scrap as he had given an undertaking on 18-10-2005 that in near future he will return back the rest scrap to the informant subject to its availability but while the argument of the DUDAC is that the accused had admitted his misappropriation in black and white on 18-10-2005, so the other evidence is immaterial in this case and the written endorsement of the accused is more than sufficient to find him guilty. 

 25. Now, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced by the learned Advocates of both the parties let us discuss and sift the evidence on record. 

 37. PW 13 Robindra Chandra Sarker, the 2 Investigation Officer of this case testified that on 15-3-2006 he was posted at Benapole Port Police Station as Sub-Inspector of Police and after the transfer of Police Sub-Inspector Abdul Jalil the case was endorsed to him for investigation and he submitted memorandum of evidence to the Police Super, Jessore and thereafter he was transferred on 6-6-2006 as such, he had returned the papers of the case to the Officer-in-Charge. There was no effective cross-examination of PW 13. 

 40. From the evidence discussed above it appears that there is no denial of the fact that PW 11 had imported 17,900 kgs iron scrap from India which entered into the Benapole Land Port on 13-9-2005 and the same were kept in shed No.8 under the custody of the present convict appellant and the said importer had engaged Jyoti International, a local C&F agent to take the delivery of the said goods on his behalf and there is no denial of the fact that at the time of taking delivery of the said goods there was a shortage of2,310 kgs of iron scrap as such the delivery was not taken place On 17-10-2005 and ultimately the same was taken place on 18-10-2005. 

 45. In this case, though the prosecution examined as many as 15 witnesses but there appears no evidence in support of the said misappropriation of the above shortage goods by this appellant. There is nothing in the record to show that he had taken the goods from the shed or he had hidden the goods elsewhere to deprive the party or he converted the goods in any manner for his own use. At the same time it is also fact that the misappropriation may not be visible always. Whenever any misappropriation is done by anybody else that will be done undoubtedly avoiding the others so that there may not be any evidence of the same. 

 46. But in this particular case, the subject matter of the misappropriation is iron scrap which are very much heavy in nature and 2,310 kgs iron scrap cannot be shifted from one place to another place keeping everybody in the dark connected with the affairs. From the evidence so far it appears that whenever any goods are kept in the customs godown, to get it out, there are many formalities and there is a chain work in taking out any goods from the shed or from the house of the port and by the single effort of a man it is always difficult to 'take out any goods from the port. 

 47. However, if this point is left out that misappropriation will, not be taken place, keeping the evidence of the same in that case also the intention of the accused is to be assessed in order to find him guilty for misappropriation. The very endorsement is going to show that he had expressed his earnest desire that whenever the shortage goods will be available he will return back the said goods to the parties concerned and from this endorsement it is clear that he had no intention to misappropriate the said goods. In this connection the case of AKM Mohiuddin vs State 7 BLT 37 = 50 DLR 447 is very much material in this case. The observation of this Court runs in the following ways: 

 48. From the materials on record, I find that though admittedly there was a shortage of 2,310 kgs iron scrap but there appears no visible evidence from the side of the prosecution that the accused had misappropriated the same for his own use or he had converted the same in any manner for his benefit. Moreso, the endorsement is going to show that he had intention to return back the goods subject to the availability of the goods. So I find it difficult to discover any intention of misappropriation of the goods by the convict appellant. 

 50. The above evidence of PW 2 is very much significant in this case that he had admitted at trial that later on they got some shortage goods. Although this evidence of PW 2 has not been corroborated by the PW 11, the importer and informant of this case. But there is a strong suggestion from the defence that since he (PW 11) got the rest goods later on he had sworn an affidavit seeking the release of the accused from the charge of the case. The PW 11 did not deny the swearing of affidavit by him in favour of the accused. So, the suggestion appears to be very much probable that since he got the shortage goods, he had sworn an affidavit to that effect. Thus, the evidence of PW 2 that later on they had got some shortage goods is very much significant and consistent with the defence case that the accused had no any intention to misappropriate the goods. So, I find that the charge of misappropriation as brought against the appellant did not stand. 

 52. Under the above facts and circumstances I am led to hold that the accused had no any intention to misappropriate the shortage goods and the prosecution by cogent and cited evidence could not prove it that the accused had misappropriated those 2,310 kgs iron scrap. 

 55. Over and above, the decision of 64 DLR 1 shows that the time limit for the investigation of the case is simply directory in nature and not the mandatory provisions of law. However, there was no any illegality in investigating of the case but on merit the judgment and the order of conviction and sentence of the appellant 'are not sustainable in' law. The trial Court without considering the legal evidence and the other aspect of the case found the appellant guilty. So, the judgment and order of conviction and. sentence of the appellant are liable to be set aside.
